questions.stem: The most fundamental economic problem in any society is
explanation_steps: Economics exists because resources are limited while human wants are unlimited – the problem of scarcity.
Every society, rich or poor, faces scarcity; poverty and inequality are consequences found only in some societies. Answer: B.
tips: Scarcity = limited resources + unlimited wants; it forces every choice in economics.

questions.stem: The question “should wheat or bicycle be produced?” is an example of
explanation_steps: The three central economic questions are: what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce.
Choosing between wheat and bicycles is choosing WHICH goods to make → what to produce. Answer: A.
tips: What = which goods and how many; How = which methods/technology; For whom = who gets the output.

similar_questions.stem: Deciding whether to use tractors or hand labour on a farm answers the question

explanation_steps: In a command (planned) economy the state owns the means of production and central planners decide what, how and for whom to produce.
Market economy = private ownership; mixed = both. Answer: B.

[Figure 1 (PPC): B is the Y-intercept of the curve and C lies on the curve; A (on the Y-axis below B) and E are inside the curve; D is outside the curve.] Which of the points in the diagram is currently <u>unattainable</u> given the economy's resources?

A concave (bowed-out) curve runs from point B on the Y-axis through point C down to the X-axis. Point A lies on the Y-axis below B (inside the curve); point E lies inside the curve; point D lies outside (to the right of/above) the curve.

questions.stem: Which of the following <u>is not</u> a capital good?

options.A: A truck used to transport goods
options.B: A loan given to an entrepreneur
options.C: A buss used to transport people
options.D: A hydroelectric dam used to produce electricity
options.E: A hammer used to break a stone

explanation_steps: Capital goods are man-made physical goods used to produce other goods and services (trucks, buses, dams, tools).
A loan is money (financial capital), not a physical means of production. Answer: B.
tips: In economics ‘capital’ means real capital (machines, tools, buildings), not money.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a <u>disadvantage</u> of a sole proprietorship?

options.B: The owner has complete control over all operations.
options.C: The owner is personally liable for all debts of the business.
options.D: All after tax profits goes to the owner.
options.E: It is easy to mobilize start-up finance.

explanation_steps: Unlimited liability: the sole owner’s personal property can be taken to pay business debts.
A, B and D are advantages; raising capital is DIFFICULT for a sole proprietor, so E is false. Answer: C.
tips: Unlimited liability and limited capital are the classic disadvantages of a sole proprietorship.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is <u>correct</u>?

options.A: Water transport is ineffective for transporting bulky goods.
options.B: Air transport is the cheapest means of transport.
options.C: Rail transport is expensive as it requires large capital investment.
options.D: Animal transport is the most effective means of transport.

explanation_steps: Railways need huge capital for tracks, stations and engines – a key disadvantage.
Water transport is best for bulky goods (A false), air is the most expensive (B false), animal transport is slow and small-scale (D false). Answer: C.
tips: Match each mode with its typical merit: water – bulky/cheap; air – fast/expensive; rail – heavy loads, high capital cost; road – flexible.

questions.stem: Which of the following <u>does not</u> decrease the supply of a particular good?

options.A: Increase in the cost of factors of production
options.B: Increase in the price of an alternative product
options.C: Decrease in the price of the good
options.D: The use of an outdated technology in production

explanation_steps: A (higher input costs), B (producers switch to the more profitable alternative) and D (outdated technology) all shift the supply curve to the left – supply decreases.
E: consumer income is a determinant of DEMAND, not of supply – it does not decrease supply.
C: a fall in the good’s own price reduces the QUANTITY supplied (a movement along the curve), not supply itself – so strictly C is also correct.
Keyed E; C also accepted.
tips: Own price → change in quantity supplied (movement along); other factors → change in supply (shift).

questions.stem: Which of the following is <u>correct</u> about insurance?
explanation_steps: G10 textbook: insurance is ‘a form of cooperation through which all those who are open to risks and losses pool their resources and compensate those who suffer a loss’ (C), and ‘the transfer of the risk of potential loss’ (B).
Its basic characteristics are ‘a. Sharing of losses … c. Risk transfer’; ‘Pooling or the sharing of losses is at the heart of insurance’ (A).
So A, B and C are all correct; only D (sharing of profits) is wrong. There is no ‘All of the above’ option.
Keyed A (the ‘heart of insurance’); B and C also accepted.
tips: Insurance = pooling + sharing of losses + risk transfer + indemnification.

similar_questions.stem: Which is NOT a basic characteristic of insurance?
explanation_steps: Insurance compensates losses; it does not create profit. Answer: D.

options.A: monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition, perfect competition.

Table 2 (Price | Quantity demanded | Quantity supplied | Excess | Pressure on price): 0 | A | 0 | 60 demand | ↓;  10 | 40 | B | 18 demand | G;  20 | 25 | C | 0 | =;  30 | D | 40 | 25 supply | ↑;  40 | 10 | E | 45 supply | H;  50 | 5 | 60 | F | ↑.

stem_tables.title: Table 2: Hypothetical demand-and-supply schedules for taxi rides in Asmara (as printed)

questions.answer: A = 60; B = 22; C = 25; D = 15; E = 55; F = 55 (excess supply); G = ↑ (upward pressure – shortage); H = ↓ (downward pressure – surplus).
explanation_steps: Excess demand = Qd − Qs; excess supply = Qs − Qd.
A: Qd − 0 = 60 → A = 60. B: 40 − B = 18 → B = 22. C: equilibrium (excess 0) → C = Qd = 25.
G: at 10 Nakfa there is excess demand (a shortage) → buyers bid the price UP → ↑.
H: at 40 Nakfa there is excess supply (a surplus) → sellers cut the price → ↓.

Note: the paper’s own arrows in the rows for 0, 30 and 50 Nakfa point the opposite way (↓ for excess demand, ↑ for excess supply). Economically, a shortage pushes price up and a surplus pushes it down.
marking_points: 0.5 point for each blank: A 60; B 22; C 25; D 15; E 55; F 55 supply; G ↑; H ↓.
Because the printed arrows (rows 0, 30, 50) are reversed, a student who follows the paper’s pattern (G ↓, H ↑) may deserve credit – teacher decision.
tips: Below the equilibrium price → shortage → price rises; above it → surplus → price falls.
Write F with its type: ‘55 supply’.

questions.stem:
What are the <u>four</u> components of expenditure used to measure GDP using expenditure method? (2 points)
2.1 ____ 2.2 ____ 2.3 ____ 2.4 ____
questions.answer: 2.1 Personal (household) consumption expenditure (C); 2.2 Gross private domestic investment (I); 2.3 Government purchases of goods and services (G); 2.4 Net exports (X − M). GDP = C + I + G + (X − M).

subparts.question: Component 1
steps: Household spending on goods and services.

subparts.question: Component 2
steps: Spending on new capital goods and inventories.

subparts.question: Component 3
subparts.answer: Government expenditure on goods and services (G)

explanation_steps: The expenditure method adds up all spending on final goods and services produced in the country.
Households spend on consumption, firms on investment, the government on goods and services, and foreigners on exports; imports are subtracted because they are produced abroad.
marking_points: 0.5 point each: consumption; investment; government purchases; net exports (exports − imports).
tips: Write ‘net exports (exports − imports)’, not just ‘exports’.

questions.stem: What is the <u>difference</u> between progressive and regressive tax? (2 points)
questions.answer: Progressive tax: the tax rate (ratio of tax paid to taxable income) INCREASES as income increases, so people with high incomes pay a larger percentage of their income (e.g. Eritrean employment income tax, 2%–30%). Regressive tax: the tax rate DECREASES as income increases, so people with low incomes pay a larger percentage of their income (e.g. a fixed head tax or many indirect taxes on necessities).
explanation_steps: G12 textbook: ‘A tax is progressive when the ratio of tax paid to taxable income increases as taxable income increases.’
‘A tax is regressive if the ratio between tax paid and taxable income decreases as income increases.’
The difference is the direction in which the average tax rate moves as income rises.
marking_points: 1 point: progressive – rate/ratio rises as income rises (higher incomes pay a larger percentage).
1 point: regressive – rate/ratio falls as income rises (lower incomes pay a larger percentage).
tips: Talk about the RATE (percentage), not the amount: under a regressive tax the rich may still pay more Nakfa, but a smaller percentage.

similar_questions.stem: A tax takes 5% of an income of 2,000 Nakfa and 5% of an income of 20,000 Nakfa. What type of tax is it?
similar_questions.answer: Proportional tax (the same rate at all income levels).
explanation_steps: The ratio of tax to income stays at 5%.

questions.stem:
Answer the following questions based on the consumption function given below: C = 100 + 0.9Y (2 points)
4.1 In the equation above, 100 refers to ____
4.2 In the equation above, 0.9 refers to ____
questions.answer: 4.1 Autonomous consumption – the level of consumption when income is zero. 4.2 The marginal propensity to consume (MPC) – 90% of each additional Nakfa of income is consumed (so MPS = 0.1).

subparts.question: 100 refers to
steps: The intercept of the consumption function.

explanation_steps: In C = a + bY, a is autonomous consumption (spending that does not depend on income, financed from savings or borrowing).
b = ΔC/ΔY is the MPC; here 0.9, so MPS = 1 − 0.9 = 0.1.
tips: The slope of the consumption function = MPC.

answer_tables.note: The textbook closes revenue first, then expenses; the order asked in the paper (expenses 5.3, revenue 5.4) is equally correct.

explanation_steps: Supplies used are an expense: move 9,000 from the asset Supplies to Supplies Expense (Supplies left = 19,000 − 9,000 = 10,000).
The 6,000 premium covers two years (2020 and 2021): one year has expired by December 31, 2020 → 6,000 ÷ 2 = 3,000 Insurance Expense; Prepaid Insurance left = 3,000.
Expenses after adjustment: Salary 34,000 + Rent 9,000 + Supplies 9,000 + Insurance 3,000 = 55,000 → debit Income Summary, credit each expense.
Revenue: debit Laundry Revenue 75,000, credit Income Summary.
Income Summary now has a credit balance of 75,000 − 55,000 = 20,000 (net income) → debit Income Summary, credit Efrem, Capital 20,000.
marking_points: 1 point each for 5.1–5.5 (correct accounts, sides and amounts).
5.3 must include the two adjusted expenses (supplies 9,000 and insurance 3,000); follow-through marks if 5.1/5.2 were wrong.
tips: Remember to close the NEW expense accounts created by the adjustments (Supplies Expense, Insurance Expense).
Net income is credited to capital; a net loss would be debited.

questions.stem:
The following information pertains to Family Electronics Plc. (5 points)
a. Cash balance per bank on March 31, 2020 was Nakfa 35,600.
b. Bank service charge for the month of March not recorded by the business was Nakfa 250.
c. Cash balance per book as of March 31, 2020 was Nakfa 31,850.
d. Outstanding cheques during the month of March 31 were Nakfa 9,300.
e. Deposits in transit as of March 31 were Nakfa 5,300.
Required: Prepare a bank reconciliation for the month of March 31, 2020.
questions.answer:
Adjusted cash balance on March 31, 2020 = Nakfa 31,600 on both sides.
Bank side: 35,600 + 5,300 − 9,300 = 31,600.  Book side: 31,850 − 250 = 31,600.

Family Electronics Plc. – Bank Reconciliation – March 31, 2020
                                          | Nakfa |   Nakfa
------------------------------------------+-------+--------
Cash balance per bank statement, March 31 |       |  35,600
ADD: Deposits in transit                  |       |   5,300
                                          |       |  40,900
LESS: Outstanding cheques                 |       | (9,300)
Adjusted cash balance, March 31           |       |  31,600
                                          |       |
Cash balance per books, March 31          |       |  31,850
LESS: Bank service charge                 |       |   (250)
Adjusted cash balance, March 31           |       |  31,600

answer_tables.title: Family Electronics Plc. – Bank Reconciliation – March 31, 2020
rows: Cash balance per bank statement, March 31

answer_tables.title: Journal entry required in the books (not asked – for practice)
rows: (To record the bank service charge for March)

explanation_steps: Bank side – items the business has recorded but the bank has not: ADD deposits in transit 5,300; DEDUCT outstanding cheques 9,300: 35,600 + 5,300 − 9,300 = 31,600.
Book side – items the bank has recorded but the business has not: DEDUCT the bank service charge 250: 31,850 − 250 = 31,600.
Both adjusted balances are equal (31,600), so the reconciliation is correct. The business then records the 250 service charge in its books.
marking_points: Bank side: 35,600 + deposits in transit 5,300 − outstanding cheques 9,300 = 31,600 – 2.
tips: Deposits in transit and outstanding cheques always adjust the BANK balance; bank charges adjust the BOOK balance.
Always prove that the two adjusted balances agree.
